newsitem.title: USA: Cinergy seeks venture in commodities trading unit.
newsitem.headline: Cinergy seeks venture in commodities trading unit.

text.p: Cinergy Corp is looking for a joint venture partner to build up its commodities trading business, Cinergy president and CEO James Rogers said Wednesday.

The Cincinnati-based utility holding company recently acquired Greenwich Energy Partners, an energy risk management and marketing firm, in its bid to build itself into one of the five biggest energy trading companies.
"I clearly envision entering into a joint venture...that will allow us to move into the top tier of traders in gas and electricity," Rogers told a group of reporters.
He said he was looking to seal a deal within the next 18 months.
He said for the company to become among the top five energy companies in five areas within five years, Cinergy would have to look at joint ventures as well as mergers.
"We continue to work today to find joint ventures. We continue to look for merger partners," he said.
The company has targeted commodities trading, wires and pipelines, and energy services to build its balance sheet and customer base.
"Figuring out a way to joint venture the services side of the business is going to be important," Rogers said.
To build its customer base from under 2 million to more than 10 million, Rogers saw big opportunities in expanding not just electricity service but billing type services.
"There may be larger margins in the back room operations than in the commodity business," he said.
He saw joint ventures as a quicker way to grow than through mergers, which require regulatory approvals that are "fraught with great risk."
But he said the company had to look at mergers and consolidations as a way to achieve short-term earnings growth.
"We're going to invest more money than we're going to make in the next three to five years," he said.
As a registered holding company, Cinergy is subject to more restrictions on its investments than many of its competitors, and is eager to see the Public Utility Holding Company Act repealed.

Rogers said the 1935 law along with other federal merger policies were limiting the ability of utilities to combine in order to compete against the giants in the industry as power markets are deregulated state by state.
House Republicans who are pushing to open all local power markets to competition do not want to repeal the holding company act without addressing broader issues in the market.

But Rogers said Congress should not hold the law hostage to other electric restructuring questions that will be harder to resolve. "I don't want to lock in the advantage of the large companies for the next five years," he said.
He said regulators had "a mindset that bigger is bad," but what the market really needed was more large companies, instead of hundreds of small utilities.
"My aspiration is to be big enough to compete with the AEP's, Southerns, and ComEds of this world," he said.
